items.title: Safety Equipment Sales: The Compliance File That Wins the Room
items.excerpt: Safety equipment deals stall on paperwork, not price. Here is why ANSI Z358.1 only binds when someone writes it into the datasheet, and how to build a compliance file you can send in an hour.
items.body:
Most [safety equipment](/pages/industrial-safety.html) manufacturers lose time on paperwork long before they lose on price. The unit is fine. The product is fine. The deal sits for three weeks because nobody can produce the one document an engineer needs to sign it off.

I have watched that happen on refineries, chemical plants and mining sites. The fix is not a better brochure. It is a compliance file you can send in an hour.

## Nobody Is Forced to Buy Your Standard

Here is the part many sellers get wrong. In the United States, OSHA requires employers to provide suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body. But in a [letter of interpretation dated April 2002](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2002-04-18-1), OSHA says plainly that ANSI Z358.1 was not adopted by OSHA, and that it has often referred employers to it as guidance. It also says OSHA has adopted no specific flow rate requirements.

So the standard is not law. It becomes the rule because an operator, an EPC contractor or an insurer writes it into the site specification. That is why the buyer's datasheet matters more than the regulation. You are not selling against a legal requirement. You are selling against whatever document the engineer has been told to follow.

> The standard becomes binding the moment someone writes it into the datasheet. Your job is to be ready for that moment.

## Know the Numbers Cold

When an engineer asks a question, the answer should take seconds. ANSI/ISEA Z358.1 2014 calls for a [shower delivering tepid water at a minimum of 20 gallons per minute](https://drs.illinois.edu/Page/Programs/EmergencyEyewashesAndShowers), which is 76 litres, for 15 minutes. An eyewash delivers at least 0.4 gallons per minute, about 1.5 litres, for 15 minutes. [Tepid means 60 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit](https://safetyequipment.org/emergency-eyewash-shower-equipment/), or 16 to 38 Celsius. The unit must be reachable within 10 seconds on the same level as the hazard. And it needs activating weekly with a proper service every year.

If you cannot say that without looking it up, the engineer notices. Confidence on the basics is what earns you the harder conversation.

## The European Side Moves Too

EN 15154 is a series, not one document, split by product type. Plumbed in body showers, plumbed in eyewash and non plumbed in eyewash units all sit in different parts. The 2006 editions of Parts 1 and 2 were [withdrawn from the end of 2025](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2006) and [replaced with 2025 editions](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025). The 2006 Part 1 was scoped to laboratory body showers only, and it said so in terms: not applicable to industrial sites.

Read that again if you sell into industry. If your datasheet still quotes the old edition, or a part that does not match the installation, a careful reviewer will find it. Check the scope of the current edition before you quote it against an industrial project. Then date your documents so nobody has to guess which version you mean.

## Build the File Once, by Operator

This is where the commercial advantage sits. Build one file per target customer and EPC. The standard they work to. Your certificates and test evidence against it. The edition. The gaps, declared up front. Buyers forgive a gap you tell them about. They do not forgive one they find.

At Hughes Safety Showers I was Export Sales Director, and the business grew from £3.9M to £6.9M. The ADNOC Offshore vendor approval engagement showed me the real problem. Safety manufacturers have no structured way to track what each operator and geography demands. Every project reinvents the question. The same pattern ran through the €1.2M [Orlen project](/pages/orlen.html) at Płock in Poland, where procurement involved several parties and nobody had patience for a compliance mistake. That experience is what became [Z358 One](/pages/z358.html), our software for ANSI Z358.1 and EN 15154 compliance and sales intelligence. If you are tracking this in a spreadsheet today, you know why.

## Compliance Tilts the Odds, It Does Not Decide Them

Being written into the specification is the [biggest lever you have](/pages/breaking-the-spec.html), and a clean compliance file is how you earn the conversation with the people who write it. It tilts the odds hard. It is not pass or fail. Plenty of safety equipment is won from the approved vendor list on the project, the budget and a sharp commercial case. But a supplier who cannot document compliance gives the buyer a reason to say no, and nobody needs to hand over that reason.

The weekly and annual obligations matter commercially too. They tell you the unit is a long relationship, not a single sale. The supplier who makes inspection and service easy is the one still in the room in year three.

If your compliance file still lives in spreadsheets and shared folders, that is the job [Z358 One](/pages/z358.html) was built for: ANSI Z358.1 and EN 15154 compliance and sales intelligence in one platform. [Book a demo](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/book-a-demo).

**Sources:** [OSHA letter of interpretation on 29 CFR 1910.151(c) and ANSI Z358.1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2002-04-18-1), OSHA, 18 April 2002. [Emergency Eyewashes and Showers](https://drs.illinois.edu/Page/Programs/EmergencyEyewashesAndShowers), University of Illinois Division of Research Safety. [Emergency Eyewash and Shower Equipment](https://safetyequipment.org/emergency-eyewash-shower-equipment/), International Safety Equipment Association. [EN 15154-1:2006](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2006) and [EN 15154-1:2025](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025), Estonian Centre for Standardisation. Checked 10 November 2026.

items.title: When to Hire a Fractional Commercial Director, and When Not To
items.excerpt: Cheaper than a full time hire is the least interesting question. Here is when a fractional commercial director is the right call for an industrial manufacturer, and when I would tell you to wait.
items.body:
Most manufacturers ask the wrong question. They ask whether a fractional commercial director is cheaper than a full time hire. Cheaper is the least interesting part. The real question is whether your business has the right problem for one.

I will tell you plainly when it works and when it does not. I would rather lose a conversation than take a retainer I cannot earn.

## When it is the right call

You have a good product and a thin international pipeline. Engineering is strong. Quality is strong. But nobody owns the commercial picture across markets, so deals drift between the MD, a salesperson and a distributor who answers email on Thursdays.

That is the gap a [fractional commercial director](/pages/fractional.html) fills. One senior person owns the pipeline, the CRM, the bids and the board reporting. Every week something moves, or we find out why it did not.

It also fits when you are [entering a new region](/pages/market-entry-for-manufacturers.html) and need relationships you cannot build in a year. Thirty years across fifteen industries means I am not starting from zero on the introductions. A full time hire who joins in month one is starting from zero, and the ramp is long.

> A distributor, a CRM and a hopeful MD is not a commercial function. It is three people hoping the fourth does the work.

### Three signs the timing is right

First, you have a sales target but no one accountable for the route to it. Second, you are already in a handful of markets and the results are uneven, with no clear reason why. Third, you are about to commit real money to a new region and want it run by someone who has done it before, not learned on your budget.

## When it is not the right call

This is the part most consultants skip. Here is mine.

**If your product is not ready, wait.** If the specification changes every month, or you cannot yet quote a firm lead time, a commercial director will spend the retainer chasing a moving target. Fix the product and the delivery promise first.

**If you want a volume cold caller, do not hire me.** A fractional director owns pipeline and relationships on six and seven figure deals. If what you need is two hundred outbound touches a week, hire a business development rep and give them a good script.

**If the MD will not hand over decisions, it will not work.** Full pipeline ownership means pricing calls, bid or no bid calls and distributor calls get made. If every one goes back to the founder for a second opinion, you have paid for a senior person and used them as an admin.

**If nothing sits behind the work, be honest about it.** I can run the commercial side. I cannot conjure tender bonds, a technical team or a delivery schedule that is not there.

**If you want results in a quarter, look elsewhere.** Industrial sales cycles are long. Forrester's State of Business Buying found that [86% of B2B purchases stall during the buying process](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024/). A good director shortens them. Nobody erases them.

## The honest comparison with a full time hire

A direct hire gives you someone who is yours every day. That has real value, particularly once the pipeline is big enough to keep a full time person busy and there is a team for them to lead. At that point a full time director is probably right, and a good fractional engagement should be building towards that decision, not avoiding it.

The fractional route wins early. Before you know which markets pay back. Before you can justify a full package and a long search. It wins on speed to a working pipeline, and it wins on the cost of being wrong. A retainer ends with notice. A bad hire costs you the search, the package and the months it takes to admit it. The full comparison is in [fractional vs full time](/pages/fractional-vs-full-time-commercial-director.html), and if the real choice is a regional hire, I have [compared those two separately](/pages/post.php?post=fractional-commercial-director-vs-regional-sales-director).

I have done the in house version too. At Brannan I joined as UK Sales Manager and ended up Global Business Development Director. The merchants were bringing in decent business, but we did not understand what they did at the back end with their customers, so I went and found out how they specified our products on projects. That is where the wins started: owning the route from product to specification to site. That ownership is the job. Whether it sits in a full time seat or a fractional one depends on where your business is today.

## How to decide in one afternoon

Write down the three deals that matter most this year. Next to each, write the name of the person who owns getting it closed. If any name is "me", "the distributor" or "we", you have a gap.

Then write down what you would do with a senior commercial lead in week one. If you can fill a page, you are ready. If you cannot, the first job is clarity, not a retainer.

That is exactly what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. It is credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. [Book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification). Or [take a 20 minute call](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/20-minute-strategy-session) and we will work out which of these you actually need.

**Sources:** [Forrester: The State Of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024/), Forrester, 4 December 2024. Checked 9 November 2026.

items.title: Nobody lost that deal to a competitor
items.excerpt: Most of the deals in a stalled forecast were never lost to a competitor. The customer simply never decided. Here is what the research says about indecision, what it looks like on an industrial deal, and what to do with the quiet deals you are carrying now.
items.body:
Ask a seller about the deals they lost last year and most will give you a name. The competitor who came in under them on price. The incumbent with the relationship. The [distributor](/pages/post.php?post=channel-partner-scoring-qualify-before-you-appoint) who had the buyer's ear.

Now look at the deals still sitting in your forecast. The quote that went out in the spring. The bid that has been in evaluation since before the summer. The customer who was positive on every call and has still not placed the order.

Nobody beat you on those. Nobody has decided anything at all. That is the deal most of us actually lose, and it rarely shows up in the loss report.

## What the research says

Dixon and McKenna, writing in Harvard Business Review in June 2022, put a number on it. Drawing on more than 2.5 million recorded sales conversations, they found that anywhere between 40% and 60% of deals are lost to customers who said they intended to buy and then did nothing.

Two things to hold alongside that figure. The authors sell a method built on this research, so they have an interest in the problem looking big. And it is cross industry, not industrial specific. Good industrial data on indecision is scarce, and I would rather say so than dress a general number up as ours.

Forrester came at it from the buyer's side. Its State of Business Buying 2024, published in December 2024 and drawn from more than 16,000 business buyers worldwide, says on Forrester's blog that 91% of purchases stall at some point in the process. Forrester's own press release the same day says 86%. The two figures conflict, the full report is for Forrester clients only, the page does not define what "stall" means, and it is buyers reporting on themselves.

Even with those caveats, the order of the causes is worth reading. Budget and price came first. Third was the buyer's own purchasing process.

> Nobody beat you on that deal. Nobody has decided anything at all.

## What it looks like on an industrial deal

You will recognise at least one of these.

The area sales manager sends the quote. The person they deal with likes it. Then someone they have never met, a buyer, a finance director, a head office category manager, has to sign, and it sits. So they chase the one person they know, who cannot make it move.

The export manager hears from the distributor that the end customer is interested. The trip goes well. Then nothing comes back, and there is no way to see past the partner to the person who actually decides.

The bid manager submits a compliant bid. It goes into evaluation and stays there for months, with no idea who is scoring it.

The sales director watches the team's biggest deals slip a quarter at a time while everyone reports that the customer is positive.

None of those is a loss to a competitor. In every one, the customer simply has not got to a decision, and usually the seller cannot see why.

## Why chasing harder rarely fixes it

The natural reaction to a quiet deal is more activity. Another follow up, another call, another revised quote. It feels like deal control. Most of the time it is pressure on the one person in the buying company who is already on your side and is not the one holding it up.

Discounting is the other reflex. Forrester's buyers did put budget and price at the top of the list, so price does matter. But a lower price on a deal nobody has agreed to buy is just a cheaper deal nobody has agreed to buy.

What moves an undecided deal is knowing how the customer is going to make the decision, and who has to be on board before they can.

In my time at Gilkes we took cycle times from 18 to 24 months down to around 12. None of it was clever. Deal control, stakeholder mapping, relentless follow ups, face to face meetings and direct engagement with the customer's technical team. The point was to know who had to move each deal, and to stop letting deals drift while we waited to hear back.

## What to do with the deals in your forecast now

- Go through every deal you are carrying and write down what the customer has done since last month. Not what you have done. What they have done.
- On every quiet deal, ask your contact one question: "who else will want a say before this is signed?" Write the names down before the next chase.
- Find out how their purchasing process actually works. Who approves, which budget it comes out of, what has to happen before an order can be raised. Forrester's buyers put their own process third on the list of reasons purchases stall.
- Agree a next step that the customer sets, with a date they own. If they will not commit to one, that tells you where the deal really is.

Most of the deals in a stalled forecast are not lost. They are undecided. The work is finding out why, early enough to do something about it.

## Bring one stalled deal

If you have a deal that has gone quiet, bring it to a free Stalled Deal Review. Thirty minutes on one stalled deal, free, and you leave with where it has actually stopped and the three things to do next. [Book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/stalled-deal-review).

If you want someone in your corner on every deal after that, that is what [The Deal Room](/pages/coaching.html) is for, one to one coaching at $500 a month.

## Sources

- [Harvard Business Review, "Stop Losing Sales to Customer Indecision", June 2022](https://hbr.org/2022/06/stop-losing-sales-to-customer-indecision).
- [Forrester, "The State Of Business Buying: Companies Still Struggle To Meet Buyer Expectations", 4 December 2024](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/state-of-business-buying-2024/).
- [Forrester, press release on The State of Business Buying 2024, 4 December 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024/).

items.title: Mining Procurement in South America: How Bechtel Buys
items.excerpt: Mining procurement in South America does not start when the tender lands. I won a $250K mining project in Chile through Bechtel by working the engineering relationship first. Here is how EPC led mining buys, and how to get in early.
items.body:
Most manufacturers think mining procurement in South America starts when a tender lands in their inbox. It does not. By then the important conversations have already happened.

I won a $250K mining project in Chile [through Bechtel](/pages/bechtel.html). There was no open tender and no beauty parade. It came from the engineering relationship and from getting the product positioned as the technical answer before procurement opened. That one result taught me more about how EPC led mining buys than any brochure about the region.

## Who actually decides

Remote mining sites do not buy like a factory. The owner sets the budget and the schedule. The [EPC contractor](/pages/epc-strategy.html) turns that into a design, a specification and a procurement plan. Then the buyers work through that plan.

That means the engineers at the EPC write the questions that procurement later asks. If your equipment fits the way the engineers have solved the problem, you arrive at procurement as the obvious answer. If you do not, you arrive as one price among several.

I will be straight about what this is. Being specified is the biggest single lever you have, and it tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not the only route. Plenty is won from the approved vendor list on the strength of the budget, the relationship with the EPC and a sharp commercial case. But the manufacturers who do the early work get to choose which fight they are in.

> By the time procurement opens, the technical argument has usually been won or lost. Your job is to be in that argument early.

## What the engineering team needs from you

Engineers at a contractor like Bechtel are carrying risk. A remote site is expensive to get wrong. Delivery into a mining region is slow. Rework is brutal. So they do not want a salesperson. They want evidence that your product will do the job, will arrive when the schedule needs it and will not become their problem.

That changes what you bring. Skip the capability deck. Bring reference installations in comparable duty. Bring clear data on performance, lead time and spares. Bring someone who can answer a technical question without going back to the factory for three days.

In Chile, that is how the relationship worked for me. I worked the engineering team and the specification, and I kept the technical case ahead of the commercial one. Price mattered, of course. It just was not where the conversation started.

## Why copper and lithium raise the stakes

Chile sits at the centre of global copper and is a major player in lithium. Both are in a growth cycle driven by electrification, and that means new capital, new expansions and EPC contractors who need reliable suppliers across a long list of packages.

That is good news for manufacturers who are ready. It is bad news for anyone who treats the region as a lottery ticket. Contractors are busy, and they do not have the time to educate a new supplier. If you cannot explain in one meeting why you fit their package, the conversation ends politely and quietly.

## A practical approach for a first move

Start by mapping the contractors, not the mines. A handful of EPCs run a large share of the major projects, and each has its own engineering centres and preferred ways of working. Learn who writes the specifications for your category and when in the project they do it.

Then get the timing right. The earlier you meet the engineering team, the more you can shape. Once the specification is issued and the tender is out, you are mostly responding. You can still win from there, but you are doing it with fewer levers.

After that, build proof that travels. One credible installation in a comparable duty is worth more than a hundred pages of capability. If you do not have one yet, say so, and be ready with the next best thing, such as test data, third party validation or a pilot arrangement.

Finally, plan for the long game. Mining capital cycles are slow. I treat the first conversation as the start of a relationship that pays out over several projects, not a single order.

## What I would do differently if I were you

I would stop asking how to get on a vendor list and start asking whose design problem I solve. Vendor registration is paperwork, and it is slow. It matters, but it does not create demand. Demand comes from an engineer who believes your product reduces their risk.

I would also stop treating [South America](/pages/south-america.html) as one market. Chile, Peru and Brazil run differently, with different local requirements and different contractor footprints. A plan that works in one will need adjusting in the next.

And I would decide early whether the region is worth it for your product. A fast, honest yes or no saves months of travel and a lot of wasted goodwill.

## Where to go from here

If you are weighing up mining in South America and want a straight answer on whether it fits your product and your route to market, that is exactly what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. If you go on to Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer, the deposit is credited in full. If I decide it is not the right fit, you get it back.

[You can book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification).

items.title: We Built a Briefing That Tells You What to Ignore, and Why
items.excerpt: Most market monitoring is a firehose. The Parteloa Intel Briefing ranks every story against your ideal customer profile, screens out the rest, and shows you the reason for each call.
items.body:
Most market monitoring tells you a lot and helps you with very little. You get forty alerts a day, and the one story that should change your week is sitting at number thirty one.

I have spent years selling industrial products across Europe, the Gulf, Africa and Central Asia. I know the feeling. You subscribe to the feeds, set up the alerts, and within a fortnight you stop reading any of them. The volume wins. The signal loses.

So we built the Intel Briefing in [Parteloa](/pages/parteloa.html) to do the opposite. It tells you what matters, and it tells you what it threw away, and why.

## A briefing judged against your profile

For every country, project and company you monitor, Parteloa writes a briefing. What happened. Why it matters to you. The angle to take.

The ranking is not by how loud the headline is. It is by how much the story matters to your own ideal customer profile. That is the whole point of defining what good looks like first. Without a written standard, every story is judged on gut feel, and gut feel gets tired by Wednesday.

> If a story does not change what you sell, you should not have to read it.

## The part most tools hide

Here is where I think we did something different. The stories that do not change what you sell are screened out. But they are not deleted. They are shown separately, with the reason.

Take a test equipment maker selling into Europe. A story about a political dispute in a market it watches. Not relevant. The briefing says so: political dispute unrelated to the sectors you sell into. Another story about a large programme, but one that targets government buyers when this maker only sells to private B2B suppliers. Screened out, with that reason attached.

You can see the judgement. You do not have to trust it blindly. If the reason looks wrong, your profile probably needs a tweak, and you find that out in minutes rather than after a missed opportunity.

## One story, once

Four outlets run the same announcement. In most tools that is four alerts. In Parteloa it is one line, marked "4 reports".

Duplicate alerts are worse than no alerts. They train you to skim. Once you skim, you miss the one that counts.

A few other changes sit in the same release:

- It reads the article, not just the headline, where the publisher allows it, before judging.
- Old tenders and closed World Bank projects no longer clutter the feed. Live and pipeline projects only.
- A "Worth adding" prompt offers companies named in your stories that you are not yet monitoring, one click away.

## Why this matters if you run more than one market

If you cover one country, you can read the news yourself. If you cover six, you cannot. Nobody can. A sales director with an installed base in the Gulf, a [distributor](/pages/post.php?post=how-to-choose-a-gcc-distributor) network in Central Asia and a new push into Africa does not need more information. They need somebody to read all of it and say: this one, today, and here is the angle.

Think about what that costs in practice. A tender opens on a Monday. An incumbent distributor loses a licence on a Tuesday. Both are buried by Thursday under repeat headlines and stories about sectors you do not touch. By the time you find them, a competitor has already made the call.

That is what the briefing is for. It sits on top of Continuous Intelligence, which watches news, filings, registries, tenders and trade press against the triggers you wrote down in your Ideal Opportunity Profile. The briefing is how the result reaches you.

## The point

Define what good looks like. Then watch the market for it. A watcher with no standard produces noise. A watcher with a standard produces a short list, a reason for every item on it, and a reason for every item left off.

If you have never written down what a great account looks like for your business, start there. It takes six questions and about five minutes. You can build your [ICP](/pages/post.php?post=your-icp-is-not-a-persona) free at parteloa.com, no card needed.

items.title: Free Zone vs Mainland: Structuring Your Gulf Market Entry
items.excerpt: Free zone or mainland is the first question most manufacturers ask about the Gulf, and the wrong one to start with. The licence should follow your route to market, not lead it. Here is how I work out who actually signs the purchase order before a dirham is spent on setup.
items.body:
## The question everyone asks first

Most manufacturers I speak to start their Gulf plan with a licence question. Free zone or mainland. It feels like the first decision, so it gets treated like the biggest one. It is not. It is a structural choice that should follow your [route to market](/pages/market-entry-for-manufacturers.html), not lead it.

I have spent thirty years selling industrial equipment into over fifty countries, and I run Venti Red from a free zone in Dubai myself. So I am not here to tell you one is good and one is bad. I am here to tell you that the licence you pick decides who can contract with you directly, and that is the part people miss.

## What a free zone gives you

A free zone company is built for holding, trading and moving goods in and out of the UAE. You typically get full foreign ownership, a simple setup and a clean base for regional sales. For a manufacturer shipping from Europe or Asia and invoicing into the Gulf, that is often enough to start.

The limit shows up when the customer is onshore. Historically a free zone entity could not trade freely with mainland customers without going through a local distributor or another mainland route. The rules have been loosening, and they differ by emirate and by free zone. Check the current position with a licensing adviser rather than trusting a blog post, mine included. The principle holds either way: your licence shapes who can contract with you and how.

## What mainland gives you

Mainland puts you inside the domestic market. Government and semi government buyers, and many large contractors, are more comfortable contracting with an onshore entity, particularly where in country value scoring counts. Foreign ownership onshore has been opened up for many activities in recent years, so the old local majority partner requirement no longer applies across the board. Activity matters, so verify it for yours.

Mainland costs more to set up and run, and it brings more compliance. It is the right answer when you will be on supplier lists, bidding to onshore buyers again and again, and building a visible local presence. It is the wrong answer when you have no pipeline yet.

> The licence follows the route to market. It never leads it.

## The EPC reality

Here is what changes the maths. On major projects your buyer is rarely the end client. It is the [EPC contractor](/pages/epc-strategy.html): Técnicas Reunidas, Saipem, Tecnimont, McDermott, Fluor, Samsung Engineering. They buy from vendors on their approved lists, and they buy globally. Plenty of those purchase orders are placed outside the UAE entirely, with delivery to site. A UK or European manufacturer can win without a UAE entity at all.

So before you spend on a licence, ask one plain question. Who signs the purchase order, and where? If the answer is an EPC procurement team in Madrid, Milan or Seoul, a UAE company may add cost and no sales. If the answer is an onshore buyer who wants local invoicing, local service and a local contract, you need a presence that supports that.

## How I work it in practice

At Hughes Safety Showers I spent nine months out of twelve in the GCC in 2024. Middle East sales rose 167% that year. The growth did not come from a better licence. It came from removing distributors that were no longer fit for purpose, moving to fire safety players who matched the buyers, and getting close to the EPC contractors directly while also bidding alongside local partners. Direct where possible, partnered where it helped. The structure served the route. Never the other way round.

That is the order I use now. Map the buyers. Work out who contracts with whom. Decide direct, distributor or both. Then choose the entity that supports it.

### Three questions before you pay for a licence

- Will your first revenue come from EPC contractors buying internationally, or from onshore buyers contracting locally?
- Do you need people on the ground, local stock or local invoicing in year one?
- Can you prove demand before you commit to fixed cost?

If you cannot answer the first one, you are not ready to choose a licence. You are ready to find out who buys.

## Where to go from here

If you are weighing up a [Gulf entry](/pages/gcc-market-entry-guide.html) and want a straight answer on structure, route and whether it is worth doing at all, book [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html). It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me. A $250 refundable deposit, credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. [Qualification](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification)

Prefer to talk first? Take a 20 minute call and we will see if it makes sense.

items.title: Why Your Competitor Keeps Winning the Same EPC Tenders
items.excerpt: Your competitor is rarely cheaper. They are easier to buy from. Here is what repeat EPC winners do before the tender, and how to find the gaps in your own bids.
items.body:
Every manufacturer I speak to has a competitor who keeps winning the same EPC tenders. Same contractors, same projects, same quiet frustration. The usual diagnosis is price. It is almost never price.

I have worked with Técnicas Reunidas, Saipem, Tecnimont, McDermott and Bechtel across thirty years of industrial sales. I have seen who wins these tenders and who does not. The pattern is consistent. The winner is rarely cheaper. The winner is easier to buy from.

## They are in the room before the tender

An [EPC contractor](/pages/epc-strategy.html) does not wake up on tender day and discover what it needs. Engineers have been shaping the scope for months. The vendor list has been argued over. Someone has already decided which suppliers are safe and which are a headache.

Your competitor is in that conversation. They have a named contact on the engineering team, and that person already understands what their product does and where it fits. When the enquiry lands, it lands on a desk where they are familiar.

Being specified is the single biggest lever in this game. It tilts the odds hard. But it is not the only route, and plenty of tenders are won from the [approved vendor list](/pages/adnoc-aramco-specification-guide.html) by the supplier with the sharper commercial case. The point is that your competitor has worked the whole chain, not just the final price sheet.

> The supplier who wins repeatedly is not the cheapest. It is the one the contractor already trusts to deliver.

## They make the contractor's risk smaller

Buyers on an EPC project are paid to avoid surprises. A late delivery on a critical path item costs the contractor far more than any saving you offered on the unit price.

So the winning supplier talks about lead time before anyone asks. They know the contractor's site date and they work backwards from it. They raise bonds, guarantees and legal terms early, and they run them in parallel with the technical work rather than in sequence.

That is how the £1.9M [Marjan](/pages/marjan.html) package for Aramco, through Técnicas Reunidas, was won. I inherited it late after a sales restructure. We closed on the operator's on site date because Borja at Técnicas Reunidas and I worked the lead time backwards, and we ran bonds and legal alongside the technical work. Around 190 units, against a date that mattered. Certainty did the work.

## They understand who actually decides

On a large project the decision is never one person. There is the engineer who writes the requirement, the procurement lead who runs the bid, the project manager who owns the schedule, and often the operator who has a view and a veto. Each one is afraid of a different thing.

The engineer fears a product that does not meet the data sheet. Procurement fears a supplier who cannot hold terms. The project manager fears delay. The operator fears being blamed later.

Your competitor has spoken to all four. They have a different answer for each, and they give it before being asked. You have probably spoken to one, and it was probably procurement, because procurement is the door that is always open.

## They bring references that fit the project

A contractor wants to know that someone like them has done this before, on something like this. A generic list of customers does not do it. A relevant reference on a comparable project, with a contact who will pick up the phone, does.

This is why wins compound. A £500K award like ADNOC Dalma gas does more than add revenue. It becomes a reference you can put in front of the next contractor. The competitor who keeps winning has simply built that library for longer than you have.

If you are the newer supplier, the answer is not to compete on the same ground. Pick the projects where your reference is strongest, or where a contractor has a problem the incumbent cannot solve, and go there deliberately.

## What to do about it

Stop asking why you lost on price. Start asking where you were absent. For your last five lost tenders, write down when you first spoke to the engineering team, whether you knew the site date, whether you had raised bonds and terms, and whether you had a relevant reference ready.

You will find the gaps are the same each time. Fix the earliest one first. It is usually the engineering conversation, and it usually needs to start a year before you think.

If you sell across more than one sector, the pattern holds. Oil and gas, power, mining, marine, rail and defence all reward the supplier who reduced the buyer's risk before the tender, not the one who cut the price on the day.

## Is it worth a conversation

If you keep losing to the same competitor, a short honest look at the buying chain usually shows why. That is what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. It is credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. [You can book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification).

items.title: SABIC and Ma'aden: Breaking Into Saudi Industrial Procurement
items.excerpt: SABIC and Ma'aden are two of the biggest industrial buyers in Saudi Arabia, and neither works like Aramco. Here is how I read the buying, why registration is a gate and not a strategy, and what I would do in the first ninety days.
items.body:
Saudi industrial procurement gets described as one thing. It is not. SABIC and Ma'aden are two of the largest industrial buyers in the Kingdom, and neither is a smaller version of [Aramco](/pages/saudi-aramco.html). Treat them like Aramco and you will waste a year.

I have a named SABIC win, a £500K order at SABIC Sharq. I have not sold into Ma'aden, so I am not going to pretend I have. What follows is how I read these buyers, built from thirty years of selling industrial equipment into process plants and the [EPC contractors](/pages/epc-strategy.html) who build them.

## Two buyers, not one

The first mistake is thinking the buyer is a procurement department. It is not. It is a plant, a project and a contractor, in that order.

A petrochemical complex or a mining and processing site has three different ways of spending money. There is the operating plant that needs spares, consumables and replacements. There is sustaining capital, where an existing asset gets upgraded or expanded. And there is the new build, which is almost always run through an EPC contractor.

Each route has different people, different timing and a different way of choosing a supplier. If your pitch does not say which route you are targeting, you are not ready to pitch.

## Start where the money is already moving

Most foreign suppliers go straight for registration. They fill in the portal, send the company profile and wait. Months later they are still waiting.

Registration matters. You will need it. But it is a gate, not a strategy. Being registered gets you permission to be considered. It does not get you considered.

The suppliers who get traction find a live project or a live plant need first. Then they work backwards to the people who own the problem. In a plant that is usually maintenance, reliability or an area engineer. On a project it is the contractor's engineering and procurement team, and sometimes the owner's project team sitting alongside them.

> Registration gets you permission to be considered. A named contact with a live problem gets you considered.

## The EPC contractor is half the answer

On any serious capital project, the contractor makes a large share of the buying decisions. I have spent years inside those relationships, with names like Técnicas Reunidas, Saipem, Tecnimont and Samsung Engineering. The pattern holds across sectors. The contractor wants a supplier it trusts, whose documents are right, whose lead time is believable and whose price will not blow up its own commercial position.

Being specified is the biggest lever you have. It tilts the odds hard in your favour. But it is not the only route. Plenty gets won from the [approved vendor list](/pages/adnoc-aramco-specification-guide.html) by the supplier who knows the contractor, has the budget case ready and makes the buyer's job easy. That is the honest position, and it is more useful than a slogan.

## What I would do in the first ninety days

Be specific about the product. A buyer at SABIC or Ma'aden does not need a brochure for everything you make. They need one clear answer to one clear problem.

Map the sites and the contractors, then pick a short list. Not twenty targets. Five that you can actually reach.

Get your documents in order before the first serious conversation. Certifications, test data, reference lists, bonds, lead times, spares policy. In Saudi Arabia a missing document does not just slow you down. It tells the buyer how you will behave after the order.

Plan for local content. In Kingdom presence is part of the commercial picture across Saudi industry, and each buyer will have its own requirements. Check the current rules directly with the buyer or through an adviser. They change, and I will not quote you a number from memory.

Then go and be there. Saudi buying runs on being seen. A call every quarter is not a relationship. Face to face, on site, with something useful to say, is.

## Where this goes wrong

The common failure is the supplier who treats the Kingdom as a single market with a single door. They appoint one agent, hand over the whole country and wait. The agent has twelve other principals and no reason to chase yours.

The second failure is confusing interest with progress. A friendly meeting at a plant is not a pipeline. A qualified project with a named decision maker, a budget and a date is.

The third is giving up at month nine. Industrial procurement in the Kingdom rewards the supplier who is still turning up in month eighteen with a better answer than the one they had in month two.

## Is it worth your time

For a lot of manufacturers, yes. The volume is real and the buyers are serious. But the honest answer depends on your product, your lead time, your margins and how much patience your board really has.

That is what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. items.title: Channel Partner Scoring: Qualify Before You Appoint
items.excerpt: Most manufacturers appoint a distributor on the strength of a good meeting, then spend two years wondering why the territory is quiet. Here are the four things I score before I sign anything, and how to spot a channel that has hit its ceiling.
items.body:
Most manufacturers appoint a distributor the way they hire a friend. Good meeting, warm handshake, strong referral, signed within a month. Then they spend two years wondering why the territory is quiet.

The appointment is the cheap part. The expensive part is the contract you cannot easily exit and the market you have handed to someone who was never right for it. Qualify first. Appoint second.

## A good meeting tells you almost nothing

Every distributor is good in a meeting. They know the buyers, they have the showroom, they mention the project they just finished. None of it is evidence that they will sell your product into your target accounts.

I have sat across the table from plenty of them. In my experience the ones who talk longest about relationships are often the ones with the thinnest pipeline. So I stopped scoring the pitch and started scoring the business.

## Score four things before you sign anything

First, **who they already sell to.** Not who they say they can reach. Ask for named accounts and the people inside them. A distributor with real access to the [EPC contractors](/pages/epc-strategy.html), the operators or the OEM buyers you need will name them without blinking. One who deflects is selling you hope.

Second, **what the rest of their line card looks like.** You are not appointing a distributor in a vacuum. You are appointing them next to everything else they sell. If a stronger competitor sits on the same shelf, you are the second call at best. If your product is the only one of its kind in the range, you are a gap they can fill.

Third, **whether the sale fits how they sell.** This is the one most people miss.

> A distributor who sells on price and availability cannot sell a product that needs a technical conversation.

At Hughes the Middle East channel ran through a PPE distributor. They sold safety equipment as a commodity item. Our product was specified into projects, so the sale was a different sale entirely. The fit was wrong from day one, and nobody had ever scored it.

Fourth, **capacity.** How many people will actually work your line? One person with forty brands is not a channel, it is a mailbox. Ask who will carry the bag, who will handle the technical queries and who will chase the EPC procurement team when the quotation goes quiet.

## Watch for the ceiling

Here is the pattern worth knowing. A distributor can look like a success for years and still be holding you back. At Hughes, the numbers through that channel landed in roughly the same place almost every year. It would reach a level and stop.

A flat number year after year is not stability. It is a ceiling. It tells you the distributor has reached the limit of what they can or will do with your product, and that there is more market out there that they are never going to touch.

I spent nine months out of twelve in the GCC that year, building relationships on the ground. I replaced the distributors who were no longer fit for purpose, built a relationship with fire safety players whose customers matched our product far better, and got close to the EPC contractors directly. Then I ran a two prong approach, direct where I could and bidding alongside the partners where it made sense. The Middle East number was up 167% in 2024.

I did not get there by working harder through the old channel. I got there by scoring it honestly and then changing it.

## Make the score a habit, not a one off

Scoring before you appoint is the minimum. The same discipline applies after. Review every partner against the same four questions each year. Who are they selling to now? Has the line card changed? Is the fit still right? Is the capacity still there?

If you only ask these questions at the start, you are working from a snapshot. Markets move, distributors get bought, key people leave and a partner that scored well in year one can be a drag by year three.

It is also why I think structured partner discovery and scoring matters. [Parteloa](/pages/parteloa.html), our market intelligence software, exists to give manufacturers a consistent way to find and score partners in a territory, so the choice rests on evidence and not on who happened to be at the exhibition. Whether you use software or a spreadsheet, the principle is the same. Write the criteria down before you meet anyone.

## What to do this week

Take your current partners, or your shortlist, and score each one on the four questions. Be blunt. If you cannot answer a question, that is your answer.

Then ask yourself one thing. If this partner never grew your number past where it is today, would you know? If the honest answer is no, you have a channel you are not managing.

If you want a straight view on whether your channel is the right one for the markets you are targeting, I run [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html). It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. It is credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the [Fractional retainer](/pages/fractional.html) if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. items.title: What an Opened Tender Really Tells You, and What It Does Not
items.excerpt: A tender notice is a signal, not a verdict. It tells you a buyer has a defined need and a live timeline. It does not tell you the race is open, or that the buyer fits your standard. Here is how to read one properly.
items.body:
A tender opens. Somebody forwards the notice to the sales team with three exclamation marks. By the afternoon, the meeting is booked and the bid team is being assembled.

Slow down. An opened tender is a signal. It is not a verdict. Most of the money wasted on tenders is spent by people who read the notice as the start of the story, when it is usually closer to the end of one.

## What an opened tender does tell you

It tells you a buyer has money, or at least approval, and a defined need. That is real. Budgets do not get released by accident, and a published scope is a written statement of what someone has decided to buy.

It tells you the timeline is now live. There is a closing date, a clarification window and a decision process. For a company that watches the market properly, that is a trigger. It is the moment a good fit becomes a live opportunity.

It also tells you who else has noticed. A public notice is public. Every competitor with an alert service saw it the same morning you did.

> A tender notice tells you the race has started. It does not tell you whether you were ever on the grid.

## What it does not tell you

It does not tell you the outcome is open. In industrial B2B, plenty of tenders are written after the real conversation has happened. The scope may reflect a design that one supplier helped shape months ago. That does not make the tender worthless for you, but it changes what you should do with it. Sometimes the right move is a bid. Sometimes it is a call to the buyer or the contractor to learn who is already close, and what the evaluation will really weigh.

It does not tell you the buyer fits your standard. A tender can be large, public and well funded, and still sit completely outside your [ICP](/pages/post.php?post=your-icp-is-not-a-persona). Wrong size, wrong sector, wrong buyer title, wrong payment behaviour. Winning a bad fit is just a slower way to lose.

It does not tell you what the buyer cares about. The document lists requirements. It rarely tells you the weighting in their heads, such as local content, delivery risk, service coverage or a partner presence on the ground. In the Gulf, that last point often decides who is credible. A manufacturer selling through partners needs to know whether their channel can actually support the bid.

And it does not tell you what happened before it. Programme announcements, funding approvals, a pre qualification round, a change in a regulator's rules. The notice is the visible tip. The signals that mattered came earlier.

## Read the notice against four profiles

This is where having a written standard changes the decision. If you have defined what good looks like, the notice becomes a short set of questions.

Does the buyer match your ICP, on sector, size, geography and the titles that sign? Does the scope map to the problem your Value Prop says you solve? Does the timing match the triggers in your IOP, or is this a late arrival into someone else's process? And is this a buyer and a project type you would want to still be working with in three years, which is the IRP question?

Four honest answers take ten minutes. They save you a bid team, a bid bond and a month of attention.

If you have not written the standard down, every tender looks attractive, because there is nothing to hold it against. That is how teams end up bidding on everything and winning the wrong things.

## Treat the tender as one signal in a chain

The best use of a tender notice is as a confirmation. Something upstream usually points to it first. A programme announcement. A budget line. A change in who holds a licence. Then the notice appears. Then, later, award news tells you who won and who is now holding stock, capacity or a grudge.

[Parteloa](/pages/parteloa.html) works this way. Continuous Intelligence reads your IOP triggers and watches news, filings, registries, tenders and trade press. Every signal is verified across at least two independent sources before it counts, and momentum is scored so a single notice sits in context with everything else around that buyer. Territory Gap and Coverage then shows whether you actually have a partner where the tender sits. Strategy Lab ranks the moves by IRP value, and partner scores can be pushed to your CRM.

None of that replaces judgement. It gives your judgement something to stand on.

## What good looks like

I have sat on both sides of these decisions, the excited forward and the sober second look. The sober look wins more often, and it costs less. Before you chase the next notice, write down what a great account looks like, what a live opportunity looks like and which relationships are worth keeping.

Then the tender stops being a siren and becomes a data point. You can build your ICP free at parteloa.com, no card needed, in about five minutes.

items.title: Winning OEM Design Ins in Marine and Power
items.excerpt: Most suppliers wait for a drawing to land on their desk. By then the design is done. Here is how I got designed in on marine and power platforms by leading with the event that forces the redesign, not the product.
items.body:
Most suppliers to marine and power OEMs wait for a drawing to land on their desk. By then the design is done. The engine builder has chosen the architecture, the supplier list is half written and you are quoting against a drawing someone else shaped.

The design in happens earlier. It happens when the engine changes. If you want to be on a marine or [genset](/pages/power-generation.html) platform for the next ten years, you need to be in the room when the engine gets redesigned, not when the parts list gets priced.

## Lead with the forcing event, not the product

Engine builders do not redesign for fun. A redesign is expensive, slow and risky. It happens when something forces it. An emissions rule changes. A power density target moves. A new customer segment demands a different duty cycle.

At Gilkes, that is exactly where the growth came from. I spotted a change in emissions regulation and worked out that engine manufacturers would be forced to update their engines. That meant the pumps would have to be redesigned for the new builds. So I went round most of the engine manufacturers globally and opened the conversation on the regulation, not on the pump.

> Nobody takes a meeting to hear about your product. They take a meeting to solve the problem a regulation just handed them.

That bought early access to the redesign work. Marine engines first, then rail, then some larger truck engines. Most of the growth from £2.5M to £15.2M came from that approach. The pump was not the pitch. The pitch was helping the engine builder get through the change.

## Talk to the technical team, and keep talking

A design in is a technical sale before it is a commercial one. The people who decide are the engineers living with the redesign. Purchasing comes later, and mostly ratifies what engineering already wants.

So you map the stakeholders properly. Who owns the cooling system. Who signs off the validation plan. Who gets blamed if the new engine runs hot in the field. Then you meet them face to face, repeatedly, and you follow up on everything. Deal control is not glamorous. It is a list of names, a calendar and the discipline to keep every thread alive.

Doing that cut our cycle from eighteen to twenty four months down to around twelve. Same product, same market, half the wait. Long cycles are not fixed. They are mostly gaps in contact.

## Expect the gateways, and handle them on your terms

Marine and power OEMs run serious quality gateways. Caterpillar was a good example. We started with their technical team on [marine engines](/pages/marine.html). When I pushed to get into their engine build programme, they asked for an open book review of our supply chain.

I pushed back. Eventually I yielded, because refusing would have ended the conversation. But I presented the information in a format that suited us. That is the skill. You do not fight every gateway and you do not hand over everything raw. You decide the shape of what you give.

Then there is GE. We picked that one up at an exhibition, where they were looking at a pump on a Caterpillar engine. It started in marine and later moved into locomotives. GE sold few marine engines a year. Big engines, low volume. That changes the economics completely. You cannot recover design effort across thousands of units.

So we charged for the design work. It was the first time in Gilkes' long history they had ever charged for pump design. I closed it. If the volume is low and the engineering is real, free design work is a subsidy you are giving a customer who has not asked for one.

## The same logic runs through power generation

The pattern repeats on gensets. I have sold into names like GE, Jenbacher, Waukesha, Cummins and MTU. The platform changes, the buyer changes, but the logic holds. Find the event that forces a redesign. Get close to the technical team early. Know the quality gateway before you meet it. Price the engineering honestly.

Being specified in at design stage is the [biggest lever](/pages/breaking-the-spec.html) you have. It tilts the odds hard. But it is not the only way in. Plenty of suppliers win from the approved list through aftermarket strength, service reach and a sharp commercial case. The design in just makes everything after it easier, including the aftermarket you keep for years.

## What to do this quarter

Pick three engine builders you want. Find the next regulation, efficiency target or duty cycle shift that touches their platform. Work out which part of your product that change forces them to rethink. Then request the technical meeting on that subject, not on your catalogue.

If you want a straight view on whether a design in strategy fits your product and your target OEMs, that is what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me. A $250 refundable deposit, credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. items.title: ICV in the UAE: Scoring Well Without Killing Your Margin
items.excerpt: ICV is a score inside the evaluation, not a gate. Here is how it works in UAE tenders, where the cheap points are, and how to avoid paying away margin for the expensive ones.
items.body:
## ICV is a scoring line, not a gate

Most foreign manufacturers hear ICV and panic. In country value sounds like a rule that says only locals can win. It is not. It is a score, and it sits inside the evaluation alongside technical fit and price.

In the UAE the National ICV Programme is run by the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. Authorised certifying bodies verify your submission against your audited financials and issue the certificate. The ministry's published guidelines set no minimum score. A low score does not ban you. It just makes you less competitive against a bidder with a higher one.

> ICV does not decide who is allowed to bid. It decides who starts the commercial review with a head start.

## What the score actually measures

The score is a percentage of how much of your spend and activity stays in the UAE economy. It is built from audited numbers, not opinions. For a goods manufacturer the formula is manufacturing cost 50%, investment 25%, Emiratization 15% and expat contribution 10%. For a service provider, third party spend takes the 50% in place of manufacturing cost. On top sits an ICV bonus capped at 5%, which draws on things like export revenue, investment growth and the number of Emiratis you employ, plus a separate technology and sustainability bonus.

Two details catch people out. First, for a service provider, spend with local suppliers is weighted by their own ICV certificates, so buying from a vendor with a valid certificate counts for more than buying from one without. Manufacturers are treated differently, and purchases from UAE manufacturers count in full. Second, a service provider in a free zone is classed as Outside UAE in the ministry's guidelines, which hurts how its certificate and spend are treated.

Read that again. Your score is partly a function of how you are set up and who you buy from, not just what you sell.

## How it shows up in a bid

[ADNOC](/pages/uae-adnoc.html) says the ICV score and improvement plan play a significant role in its commercial evaluation, that higher scores give an edge, and that award is not based on ICV alone. Other buyers may treat it differently, so read the tender documents.

Here is the part most exporters miss. What you buy feeds your own score, and the same is true for a main contractor buying from you. So when I talk to an EPC about a package, local content can be on the table even if the end user never mentions it. A supplier who arrives with a credible local content story is easier to say yes to.

On the ADNOC Dalma gas work, at £500K, and on Borouge, at £250K, local content was part of the commercial conversation, not an afterthought on the bid form. I will not narrate the detail. The point is that the supplier who raises it first looks organised.

## Scoring well without killing your margin

This is where I see money burned. A manufacturer panics, signs a weak local partner, and gives away margin to buy a few ICV points. That is the wrong trade.

Start with the cheap gains.

- Get certified. Arriving with no certificate hands the points to someone else.
- Clean up your books. If your accounts do not separate UAE sourced purchases from imports, the certifier cannot credit what you already do.
- Look at where you already spend in the UAE. Logistics, packing, testing and service can count and cost you little.
- Buy from certified local vendors where the price is fair. Spend with an uncertified vendor scores lower.

Then look at the structural moves, but cost them honestly.

- A local assembly or finishing step can lift your score. Price it against the margin it protects, not just the points it earns.
- A distributor or service partner with a strong certificate can carry part of the load. Choose on capability first. A good partner with a high score is worth having. A weak partner with a high score is a liability. [Parteloa](/pages/parteloa.html), our market intelligence software, scores partners too, because finding the right ones is slow when done by hand.
- Emiratization counts for up to 15% of the score, but only hire where the role is real.

## What I would do before the next bid

Do not let ICV be a surprise in week three of a tender. Find out which buyers in your pipeline score it and how. Get your certificate sorted before the invitation lands. Then work out how many points you can earn at low cost and stop there. Chasing the last ten points can cost more than the contract is worth.

And be clear on one thing. A strong ICV score helps. It is not a substitute for the technical case, [the EPC](/pages/epc-strategy.html) relationship or a sharp commercial offer. Plenty is won with a middling score by the supplier who got everything else right.

If you are weighing a UAE bid and want a straight view on whether the ICV maths works, that is what [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is for. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. It is credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. [Book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification). Or grab a 20 minute call and we will talk it through.

**Sources:** [National ICV certification guidelines for suppliers, Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, September 2025](https://moiat.gov.ae/-/media/site/moiat/programs/icv-formula/icv-supplier-certification-guidelines-sep-2025-v1.ashx). [ICV formula, Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology](https://moiat.gov.ae/en/programs/icv-formula). items.title: The Commercial Architecture Behind Every Won Contract
items.excerpt: International tenders are rarely lost on price. They are lost on the commercial structure around the product. Here are the five parts that decide who wins, and where manufacturers leave gaps.
items.body:
## Most tenders are lost before the price is opened

When a bid fails, the post mortem is nearly always about price. Too high, too slow, too late. I rarely believe it. In thirty years and more than fifty countries, I have seen price decide a contract far less often than the structure around it.

A won contract is not one thing. It is five things built in the right order, and a weak link in any of them shows up at the worst moment. I call it the commercial architecture. Most manufacturers build the product and hope the rest assembles itself.

> A tender is a commercial structure that happens to include a product.

## The five parts

**Technical qualification.** Can the buyer's engineers sign off on you without a fight? This is where being specified helps most. It tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not the only route, and plenty is won from the [approved vendor list](/pages/adnoc-aramco-specification-guide.html) on the strength of everything else on this list.

**Commercial structure.** Payment terms, bonds, warranty, lead time and delivery terms. These are not details to sort out after award. On a big package they are the contract. A supplier who can say yes to a performance bond and a tight delivery date without a three week internal debate is already ahead.

**Stakeholder coverage.** The engineer who qualifies you, the buyer who runs the process, the project manager who owns the date and the person who signs. They want different things. Most bids talk to one of them.

**Timing.** Where in the project are you? Engaging during design is a different sale from quoting on a finished package. You can win at either stage, but you need to know which one you are in.

**Risk allocation.** Who carries the risk if something slips? Buyers do not just buy a product. They buy a reduction in what could go wrong for them.

## What running it in parallel looks like

On the [Saab naval](/pages/saab.html) tender in Sweden, the work ran across several gates. Technical qualification and commercial negotiation ran at the same time, not one after the other. We stayed in front of the buyer through every gate rather than waiting for the next to open. That was worth $650K, and it opened Scandinavian defence and government markets the business had not touched before. Nammo in Norway, at $500K, followed the same pattern.

The lesson is not that defence is special. The lesson is that nobody on that tender was surprised by the commercial terms, because the commercial conversation started when the technical one did.

Compare that with the usual approach. Win the technical argument. Hand over to someone in finance. Discover the buyer wants a bond you cannot issue and a delivery date you cannot hit. Two months later, you are the second choice.

## Getting in ahead of the process

The [Bechtel mining](/pages/bechtel.html) win in Chile, $250K, came the same way. It was won through the engineering relationship, positioned as the technical solution before procurement formally opened. By the time the buyers ran their process, the question was not whether we could do it. It was how to paper it.

That is the point about timing. Architecture built early costs you conversations. Architecture built late costs you the contract, or your margin.

## Where manufacturers lose

I see the same four gaps again and again.

- The sales team qualifies the technical fit and never asks who signs.
- Lead time is quoted from the factory, not worked backwards from the buyer's site date.
- Bonds, legal and payment terms are treated as admin, not as part of the proposition.
- One champion inside the buyer carries the whole bid, and when they move on, so does the deal.

None of these are product problems. A better product does not fix them.

## What to do with it

Before the next bid, write the five parts down on one page and be honest about which are covered and which are hope. Where you have a gap, fix it now, not after the invitation to tender lands. Ask who signs. Work the lead time backwards. Get your legal and finance people on the first call, not the last.

items.title: Doing It Again Next Door: Market Sequencing for Exporters
items.excerpt: Most exporters pick their second market by who shouted loudest. The first market is a sample, and it should decide where you go next. Here is how to sequence on fit and live signals, not size or proximity.
items.body:
Most exporters pick their next country the same way. Someone saw a trade show. A [distributor](/pages/post.php?post=how-to-choose-a-gcc-distributor) sent a friendly email. A competitor announced a win there. The board nods, because the market is big and the story is good.

That is not sequencing. That is following the noise.

The first market you enter teaches you what a great account looks like. The second market should be chosen by what you learned. If it is chosen by who shouted loudest, you have thrown the lesson away.

## Your first market is a sample, not a strategy

Say you have built a position in the UAE selling engineered equipment through two distributors. After a couple of years you know things. Which buyer titles actually sign. How long the cycle really runs. Which type of partner brings you projects and which only brings you enquiries.

All of that is evidence. The question for market two is simple. Where else does the same evidence apply?

Saudi might look like the obvious next door neighbour. It may well be. But "it is close" is a geography argument, not a fit argument. If your best accounts in the UAE are contractors tied to large project owners, you want the market with the same structure, not the market with the same border.

> Proximity is a map. Fit is a standard. Only one of them tells you where to go next.

## Score the next market against what you wrote down

This is where the six question [ICP](/pages/post.php?post=your-icp-is-not-a-persona) Builder earns its keep. Your answers describe your best customers, the problem you solve, what makes them start looking, who is a bad fit, why they choose you and what keeps them loyal. Those become four frameworks. ICP, Value Prop, IOP and IRP.

Now you have a standard. Hold each candidate market up against it.

How many accounts in that country match your ICP on sector, size and buyer title? Do the triggers in your IOP actually occur there, programme announcements, tenders opening, an incumbent losing a licence? Are there partners who look like the ones you would still want in three years, which is the IRP question? And do your red flags show up early, such as a market where every route to customer runs through one gatekeeper you have no leverage over?

Five minutes of gut feel will give you an answer. Scored properly, you get a ranking with reasons. When two markets look close, the reasons are what break the tie.

## Sequence on signal, not on size

Market size is the most overrated number in export planning. A large market where you match forty accounts and see two live triggers a quarter is a worse next move than a smaller one where you match twelve accounts and the triggers are firing now.

Timing is part of the sequence. Europe, [the Gulf](/pages/gcc-market-entry-guide.html), Central Asia and Sub Saharan Africa all move on different rhythms. A tender cycle in one region can open while another is still waiting on funding. Watching for triggers across several candidate markets at once tells you which door is opening, instead of which door looks grandest.

This is what Continuous Intelligence does in Parteloa. It watches news, filings, registries, tenders and trade press against your IOP triggers, verifies each signal across at least two independent sources and scores the momentum. Territory Gap and Coverage then shows where you have no presence against where the signals are building.

## Decide what you will not do next

Sequencing is as much about the market you leave for later. Write down the no list before the meeting. Which countries fail your red flags. Which ones need a partner type you have already decided not to work with. Which ones depend on a single buyer.

Every market you rule out on paper is a market you do not spend a year and a travel budget discovering the same thing the hard way.

## What good looks like

I have built markets from zero more than once, and the pattern holds. The exporters who compound are not the ones who enter the most countries. They are the ones who treat each entry as an experiment, record what the standard says, check the result against it and carry the lesson forward.

Your next market should look like your best existing one in the ways that matter, and show live signals right now. If it passes both tests, go. If it passes neither, it is a distraction with a flag on it.

Start by writing the standard down. You can build your ICP free at parteloa.com, no card needed, and score your next market against it before anyone books a flight.

items.title: A Fractional Commercial Director for UK or Gulf Market Entry
items.excerpt: Entering a new market is a commercial build, not a hire. Here is what a fractional commercial director does for a manufacturer moving between the UK and the Gulf, and when it is the wrong answer.
items.body:
## Entering a market is a commercial build, not a hire

Most manufacturers treat a [new market](/pages/market-entry-for-manufacturers.html) as a recruitment problem. Find a person, give them a patch, wait. It works about as often as you would expect. The first year in a new market is not selling. It is building the commercial machine that selling depends on, and that is a different job from the one most new hires are given.

I have built markets from zero three times. The pattern holds whichever way you are travelling, a British manufacturer heading for the Gulf or a Gulf manufacturer heading for [the UK](/pages/united-kingdom.html). The geography changes. The work does not.

## What the work actually is

Before the first serious order, somebody has to do five things. Map the live projects or the live buyers and find out who runs them. Decide direct or distributor on evidence, not on whoever answered the first email. Get in front of the people who influence the purchase before the tender is written. Build the paperwork the buyer will ask for, from certifications to bonds to realistic lead times. Then run a pipeline with a cadence high enough that deals move every week.

In the Gulf, that means the EPC contractors, the Técnicas Reunidas and Tecnimont and Saipem type accounts, and the operators behind them. Vendor approval is advisory. It is slow and hard, and I would never tell you I can get you approved by ADNOC or Aramco. The real route to revenue is influence on the specification and the contractors who carry your name into the bid.

In the UK it is a different cast. Merchants, contractors, consultants and distributors, each with their own buying habits. The skill is the same. Find who really decides, and get there early.

> A hire fills a seat. A fractional director builds the machine the seat depends on.

## Why one person for both directions

I am based in Dubai and I operate internationally. In the last year I closed two deals in the UAE and twenty five in other markets, mostly Europe. The Gulf is one market among many for me, never the headline. That matters here, because a manufacturer moving in either direction needs someone who has already seen both buying cultures from the inside.

At Gilkes I did not open conversations with engine builders about pumps. I opened them on the emissions regulations that were forcing engine redesigns. That bought early access to the design work, and it cut the sales cycle from eighteen to twenty four months down to around twelve. Same lesson in any market. Lead with the thing the buyer already has to deal with, not with your product.

At Hughes I removed distributors that were no longer fit for purpose and rebuilt the route to market around the fire safety players, with a direct approach alongside. The flat number a distributor delivers year after year is not stability. It is a ceiling. A [fractional director](/pages/fractional.html) finds the ceiling and breaks it.

## What you get each month

You deal with me, start to finish, not a rotating team. The retainer covers weekly commercial execution, so live deals move or we find out why they have not. I own the CRM, so every deal is tracked, staged and actioned. I represent you in region when it matters. You get monthly board reporting you can actually act on, and tender strategy through to submission and follow up.

There is no recruitment fee, no relocation, no twelve month ramp and no notice period risk. You get the relationships that already exist, from week one.

## Being specified is the lever, not the gate

I will say this plainly because it gets overstated. Being written into the specification is the biggest single lever in industrial sales and it tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not pass or fail. Plenty of business is won from the approved vendor list on the strength of the EPC relationship, the budget and a sharp commercial case. A good commercial director works all of those at once.

The same discipline applies to your channel. Score every distributor against a written standard before you appoint, not after. Partner discovery is one of the jobs Parteloa does, and it is the step most exporters skip, then pay for two years later.

## When it is the wrong answer

If you already have a working pipeline and nobody to work it, hire a sales director. If the product is not ready for the market, fix the product. If you want someone to hold a business card in Dubai or Manchester and report back, I am not your person.
