items.title: UK to Gulf Export Under the FTA: Tariffs, Timelines and Route to Market
items.excerpt: The UK and GCC free trade agreement is concluded, not yet in force. Here is what is agreed on tariffs and timelines, where the duty saving helps, and why your route to market is still the real job.
items.body:
A tariff schedule is not a sales plan. If you make things in Britain and want to sell them into the Gulf, the new UK and GCC free trade agreement is good news. It is also a reason to get disciplined, not a reason to get excited.

Here is what is actually on the table, what is not, and what I would do with the next twelve months.

## What is agreed, and what is not live yet

The UK and the six GCC states concluded negotiations on 20 May 2026. Concluded is not in force. The legal text still has to be finalised, and the agreement only takes effect once [the UK](/pages/united-kingdom.html) and every GCC member state complete ratification. In the sources I checked, none gives a signature date or an entry into force date. Anyone who quotes you one is guessing.

What is public is the shape of it. Tariffs are eliminated on around 93% of current UK exports, worth an estimated £580 million a year in duties. Around £360 million of that comes off immediately on entry into force. The GCC fully liberalises 90% of its tariff lines on UK goods within ten years, and products on a phased schedule follow five or ten year timelines. For products on a phased schedule, the agreement also stops GCC tariffs rising before they are removed. This is a UK agreement, not an EU one.

> The tariff clock and the readiness clock are different clocks. You cannot move the first one. You can start the second today.

## Where the duty saving actually helps

Be honest about your product. If you sell on price in a competitive category, a lower duty line goes straight to your landed cost and your margin. That is real money and you should model it by product, not by headline.

If you sell engineered equipment into a project, the duty is rarely the reason you win or lose. I have worked on a £500K ADNOC Dalma gas package, a £500K SABIC order and a Borouge order of £250K. None of those turned on a percentage point of customs duty. They turned on lead time, documentation, the [EPC contractor](/pages/epc-strategy.html) and a commercial case the buyer could defend internally.

Rules of origin matter too. Goods must be wholly obtained or sufficiently transformed in the UK or [the GCC](/pages/gcc-market-entry-guide.html), with product specific rules for third country inputs. If your supply chain runs through several countries, check that now. UK exporters can self certify origin after registering, which helps, but only if the paperwork behind it is clean.

## The route to market is still your problem

A free trade agreement gets your goods to the border cheaper. It does not put your name in front of the people who decide.

In the Gulf that means the EPC contractors and the operators. Técnicas Reunidas, Tecnimont, Saipem, McDermott, Samsung Engineering. Being written into the specification is the single biggest lever you have, and it tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not the only route. Plenty is won from the approved vendor list on the strength of the EPC relationship, the budget and a sharp price and lead time. But none of it happens until the right engineers and procurement teams know you exist.

Vendor approval with ADNOC or Aramco stays slow and hard whatever the tariff schedule says. I advise on it, I do not promise it, and neither should anyone else. The real revenue sits in influencing the specification and working the contractors.

Government procurement is worth a look as well. The agreement creates legally binding commitments with Bahrain and the UAE, and the other four GCC states have to assess their participation within two years. That is a door, not a contract.

## What I would do before the tariffs move

First, pick the sector and the country where you already have a credible reference. Oil and gas gets the attention, but construction, manufacturing, defence, marine, rail, mining and power all buy British product. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar behave very differently. Do not try to take all three.

Second, decide direct or distributor, and be ruthless about it. The expensive mistake is appointing the first partner who returns your call and finding out two years later that they sold nothing. Score candidates against a written standard before you sign. Partner discovery is one of the things Parteloa does, and it is the work most exporters skip.

Third, build the paperwork. Origin evidence, certifications, a bond and guarantee position, realistic lead times. You will be asked for all of it, and the buyer will not wait while you find it.

Fourth, run the numbers on what the duty saving is worth to your customer, not just to you. A saving you can show on their landed cost is a commercial argument. A saving you quietly keep is only margin.

If you are weighing a Gulf move and want a straight answer on whether it makes sense for your product, [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html) is a paid yes or no call, direct with me. It is a $250 refundable deposit, credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you proceed, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. [You can book it here](https://cal.com/scott-robinson-hn8vga/qualification). Or take a 20 minute call and we will talk it through.

**Sources:** [UK and GCC trade deal: conclusion summary](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-gulf-cooperation-council-gcc-trade-deal-conclusion-summary/uk-gulf-cooperation-council-gcc-trade-deal-conclusion-summary--2), GOV.UK, updated 10 June 2026. [UK and Gulf strike historic multi billion pound trade deal](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-and-gulf-strike-historic-multi-billion-pound-trade-deal), GOV.UK, 20 May 2026. The tariff figures are UK government estimates. Checked 7 November 2026, when neither page gave a signature or entry into force date.

items.title: Relationship Selling in the GCC vs the Agenda Driven West
items.excerpt: The West opens with an agenda. The Gulf opens with a relationship. I learned the difference at the Big 5 show in November 2018, on my first ever trip to the region, and it changed how I sell.
items.body:
In November 2018 I walked onto the Big 5 show in Dubai. It was my first time in the region. The furthest east I had ever been was Egypt, on holiday. I had never done a day of business in [the Gulf](/pages/gcc-market-entry-guide.html).

I came home with a different view of how selling works. Here is what I learned, and why it still decides who wins and who waits.

## Two Ways of Starting a Conversation

I started in direct sales in the mid 90s. The Western model I grew up in is agenda driven. You agree a purpose, you agree next steps, you leave with a date in the diary. It is efficient and I have closed plenty of business that way. I still do.

The Gulf runs differently. You build the relationship first. Family, life outside work, football, Formula One, whatever common ground you can find. That trust is what earns you the right to pitch. Nobody is being slow or rude. The relationship is the qualification step, and it comes before the commercial one.

Each GCC country has its own flavour. The principle is the same across all of them.

> In the West the agenda earns you the meeting. In the Gulf the relationship earns you the agenda.

## What I Did on the Stand

After one day I knew the stand was the wrong place to sell. So I did not try to drill into projects with people walking past. I told my MD I was coming back in two weeks, and I booked about four days of office meetings.

That was the whole plan. Show up, meet people on their ground, and let the conversation start somewhere other than the product.

My first meeting was on a construction site in JVT. There was barely anything built there compared with today. I drank my first Arabic coffee. The Lebanese contact I met struggled with my accent.

Nothing came of that meeting.

It still set up everything that followed. It opened the door to a great many meetings and a lot of business in the region over the years that followed. The return came later and it was far bigger than any single order.

## Why Western Teams Get This Wrong

Most overseas manufacturers do the opposite. They fly in with a deck, a target list and a three day agenda. They ask for the specification, the budget and the decision date in the first hour. On paper that is professional. In the room it reads as someone who wants something and has not earned it yet.

Then they go home and wait. A tender comes out, they price it, and they wonder why the same names keep winning.

The names that keep winning were in the room long before the tender. They knew the engineers, the buyers and the people two levels above them. When a problem came up, they were the first call.

This matters beyond the Gulf. The same pattern runs through EPC procurement with firms like Técnicas Reunidas, Saipem and Tecnimont, and through any market where people buy from someone they trust. The agenda driven approach works when the buyer already has a need and a process. The relationship approach works earlier, when the need is still forming and somebody has to shape it.

## How to Run It Without Wasting Years

Relationships take time, and time costs money. So you need a method, not just good intentions.

First, separate the show from the selling. Use the exhibition to meet people and book dated meetings in their offices. Do not try to close on the stand.

Second, go back quickly. I went back in two weeks. A short gap shows you meant it. A long one tells them you were collecting business cards.

Third, accept that the first meeting may produce nothing, and plan for that. Judge the trip by who you met and what they would say about you afterwards, not by the quote count.

Fourth, keep the commercial discipline. Relationship first does not mean commercial last. Once you are trusted, lead times, bonds, terms and pricing still have to stand up. Trust gets you in the conversation. A sharp commercial case wins it.

## The Takeaway

If your Gulf strategy is a deck and a list of tenders, you are playing the Western game in a market that plays a different one. Change the order. Build the relationship, then bring the agenda.

items.title: How I Grew a Safety Equipment Manufacturer From £3.9M to £6.9M
items.excerpt: A flat number through a distributor is not stability, it is a ceiling. Here is how I took Hughes Safety Showers from £3.9M to £6.9M by changing the channel, getting close to the EPCs and spending nine months a year in the GCC.
items.body:
I was Export Sales Director at Hughes Safety Showers, and the business grew from £3.9M to £6.9M. What moved it was who we sold through, who we sold to, and how much of the year I spent standing in the markets instead of managing them from a desk.

Here is what actually moved the number.

## A Flat Number Is Not Stability

The first thing I noticed was the pattern. Through the incumbent distribution, the business landed on roughly the same figure almost every single year. It would climb to a level and stop. Nobody questioned it, because a steady number feels safe.

It is not safe. It is a ceiling. When a channel produces the same result year after year, the channel has told you its capacity. Either the [distributor](/pages/post.php?post=how-to-choose-a-gcc-distributor) has reached the limit of what they can sell, or they have reached the limit of what they will sell for you. Both mean the same thing. You have outgrown them, or they were never the right fit.

I pointed it out and moved on. That sentence sounds quick. It was not. It meant removing distributors that were no longer fit for purpose, and that is never a comfortable conversation.

> If your distributor delivers the same number every year, you are not looking at stability. You are looking at their ceiling.

## The Wrong Channel for the Right Product

The incumbent in the Gulf was a PPE distributor. They sold [safety equipment](/pages/industrial-safety.html), but they sold it the way you sell gloves and goggles. Fast, in volume, off the shelf. Safety showers and eyewash stations are a different sale. They are specified into a project, they sit on an engineer's datasheet, and they get bought by contractors building plants, not by a stores manager topping up stock.

I spotted that the fire safety sector lined up far better. That sector sold into projects and understood a project sale. So I built a strong relationship with fire safety players and let the PPE channel shrink to what it was good at.

That is the lesson I would give any manufacturer. Do not ask whether your distributor is good. Ask whether they sit in the same part of the buying process as your product.

## Nine Months Out of Twelve

In 2024 I spent nine months of the year in the GCC. Not on a flying visit every quarter. On the ground, building relationships. The result was not a campaign. It was presence.

I got properly close to the [EPC contractors](/pages/epc-strategy.html) working in the region. Técnicas Reunidas, Samsung, Saipem, McDermott, Wood, CNPC, Tecnimont and Target Engineering. These are the people who decide what goes on a project, and they will not give their time to someone they have never met.

That presence let me build a two prong approach:

- Go direct to the contractor wherever the project allowed it.
- Bid alongside the fire safety players where their position gave us the better route.

Running both mapped the market properly. It gave us the best chance of winning each job. And it opened up projects we were never even getting to pitch for while we ran purely through distribution. Those jobs had been there all along. We just had no route into the conversation.

## What the Numbers Said

Middle East sales rose 167% in 2024. In the same period we won major projects in Poland and Norway, and I developed the existing distributors in both countries so they could win more business themselves. That matters. Fixing a channel does not always mean replacing it. In some markets the right move is to equip the partner you already have.

2024 was also the first time in my time at the company that export sales overtook home market sales. That is what happens when you stop treating export as an add on and start treating it as a market build.

## Being Specified Helps, But It Is Not the Whole Game

Getting close to the EPCs mattered because being specified is the biggest lever in project sales. It tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not the only route. Plenty of work is won from the approved vendor list, on the strength of the relationship, the budget and a sharp commercial case. The point of being on the ground was to be in the room for all of it.

## What To Take From This

If your growth has gone flat, check three things before you blame the market.

- Is your channel sitting in the same part of the buying process as your product?
- Do you know the contractors who actually decide, and do they know you?
- Are you present, or are you managing by report?

Working out which distributors fit a product like this takes real intelligence on who is actually active in the market. Partner discovery and scoring is one part of what Parteloa does, so you stop appointing on a hunch.

items.title: Turning Safety Compliance Into a Sales Advantage: ANSI Z358 and EN 15154
items.excerpt: Most safety manufacturers treat compliance as a hurdle. The ones who treat it as a sales tool win the jobs where buyers are afraid of being wrong. Here is how ANSI Z358.1 and EN 15154 become a commercial advantage, not just paperwork.
items.body:
Most safety equipment manufacturers treat compliance as a hurdle. A certificate you collect so the product is allowed in the room. I treat it as a sales tool, and the manufacturers who do the same win more of the jobs where buyers are nervous.

Safety showers and eyewash stations are a perfect example. Nobody buys one for fun. They buy because a hazard assessment says they must, and because a mistake on site is expensive in every sense. That changes who you are really selling to.

## The Buyer Is Afraid of Being Wrong

Think about who signs off a [safety shower](/pages/industrial-safety.html) on a refinery, a chemical plant or a mining site. It is rarely the person who will ever use one. It is an EHS manager, an engineer on the EPC, a procurement lead who has been told the unit must meet the standard. All of them share one fear. Putting their name against kit that fails an audit or fails a person.

So the product that wins is often the one that makes their decision easiest to defend. Not the cheapest. The one with the cleanest compliance story.

> A buyer who is afraid of being wrong will pay for the supplier who removes the doubt.

## Two Standards, Two Different Worlds

ANSI Z358.1 is the US standard for emergency eyewash and shower equipment. EN 15154 is the European series covering emergency safety showers and eyewash units. They overlap in intent, but they are different documents with different requirements and different test routes. Meeting one does not automatically mean you satisfy the other.

That sounds like a technical footnote. It is a commercial opening.

On global projects the standard named depends on where the engineering was done, who owns the site and which operator is paying. A US based EPC might write ANSI into the datasheet. A European operator or contractor might write EN 15154. On a Gulf project it depends on the contractor and the client standard, so you ask rather than assume.

Most manufacturers know their own certification and little else. When a datasheet names a standard they do not hold, they either go quiet or quote anyway and hope. The ones who can say, quickly and with evidence, exactly which standard their range meets and where, look like the safe pair of hands.

## Be Ready Before They Ask

Here is where compliance becomes a sales advantage rather than paperwork.

Have your test evidence and certification organised by standard, by product and by region. Not buried in a folder somewhere. Ready to send in an hour when an engineer asks. A deal can stall for weeks because a supplier cannot produce the one document a reviewer needs. The product is fine. The paperwork is not.

Know which standard each target customer and each EPC actually works to. Ask early. It is a simple question and it tells the buyer you understand their world.

Be honest about gaps. If you do not hold a certification a project needs, say so, and say what you will do about it. Buyers forgive a gap that is declared. They do not forgive one they discover.

## Compliance Opens Doors Into Specifications

Being written into the specification is the biggest lever you have in industrial sales. It tilts the odds hard. It is not the only route, and plenty of safety equipment is won from the [approved vendor list](/pages/adnoc-aramco-specification-guide.html) on the project, the budget and a sharp commercial case.

But compliance is how you earn the conversation with the people who write specifications. Engineers will not put a product in a document if they cannot defend it. Give them a clear compliance file and you make it easy to say yes.

I got close to this at Hughes Safety Showers, where I was Export Sales Director and the business grew from £3.9M to £6.9M. The work around the ADNOC Offshore vendor approval engagement showed me something I could not unsee. Safety manufacturers have no structured way to track compliance requirements across different operators and geographies. Every project reinvents the question. That gap is exactly what Z358 One was built to close, a software platform that combines ANSI Z358.1 and EN 15154 compliance with sales intelligence.

The [Orlen](/pages/orlen.html) refinery project in Poland, worth €1.2M, was the same story at scale. Safety shower and eyewash provision into one of the largest refineries in Central Europe, with several parties involved in procurement and no tolerance for compliance mistakes.

## Make Compliance Part of the Pitch

Do not leave your compliance until the technical submission. Put it in the first conversation. Lead with the standard the customer works to and show that you know the difference between that and the alternative. It changes how you are perceived. You stop being a vendor with a catalogue and become someone who understands the risk the buyer is carrying.

This applies well beyond showers and eyewash. Anywhere a product is bought to protect people, whether in oil and gas, chemicals, mining, marine or construction, the compliance story is part of the product.

items.title: Getting Precision Kit Specified by Engineers and Labs
items.excerpt: Precision kit gets chosen long before anyone raises a purchase order. The engineer or lab manager who writes the requirement decides what good looks like, and procurement buys against it. Here is where that requirement actually gets written, and how to be in the room when it does.
items.body:
Precision kit gets chosen long before anyone raises a purchase order. The engineer or lab manager who writes the requirement decides what good looks like, and procurement then buys against it. If you want to sell more instruments, test systems or electronics into a new market, that is where your effort has to go.

My last piece covered the considered buy, how the purchase gets justified and won. This one is about the step before it. Getting written in.

## Where the Requirement Actually Gets Written

Every precision buy starts as a document. In a regulated lab it is a user requirement specification. In a test house it is the test method and the procedure behind it. On an engineering project it is the equipment datasheet the design team issues before procurement opens.

Pharma makes the point clearly. Under EU GMP Annex 15, equipment requirements are defined in a user requirement specification, and that document stays the reference point through design, installation, operational and performance qualification. Whoever shaped the URS shaped the buy. Measurement range, accuracy, data integrity, service response. It is all in there before a single quote is requested.

Other sectors are less formal, but the pattern holds. Semiconductor fabs, packaging test labs, aerospace QA, research groups, utilities. Someone technical writes down what the instrument has to do. That moment is your window.

## Why Engineers Do Not Buy From Salespeople

Engineers and lab managers buy from people who help them get the requirement right. Not from people chasing a meeting to talk about product.

The fastest way I know into a technical buyer is to lead with their problem, not your datasheet. A new standard coming in. A test method changing. An audit finding they need to close. A throughput problem on the line. At Gilkes we opened conversations with engine manufacturers on emissions regulation, not on pumps, and that is what bought us early access to the redesign work. Different product, same principle. Regulation and method changes force a rewrite of the requirement, and whoever is in the room when it is rewritten has the advantage.

In practice your application engineers matter more than your salespeople in the early stage. Get them in front of the people writing the method. Offer a demo on the customer's own samples. Help draft the acceptance criteria. Be the person the engineer rings when they are not sure what tolerance to write.

> The engineer who writes the requirement is your real customer. Procurement is the process that follows.

## What Bechtel in Chile Taught Me

Mining in Chile is remote, high value and led by [the EPC](/pages/epc-strategy.html). Specifications are written by the engineering team long before anything is bought, and Bechtel is one of the most rigorous EPC environments anywhere.

I won a $250K mining project there. Not through an open tender. Through the engineering relationship and the specification, getting the product positioned as the technical solution with the engineers before procurement opened.

That was not [instrumentation](/pages/electronics-instrumentation-test.html), but the mechanism transfers straight across. A lab, a fab and a mine have the same shape. Technical people define the need. Commercial people buy against it. If you only ever meet the commercial people, you are selling against a requirement somebody else shaped.

## The Biggest Lever, Not the Only One

Being written in is the single [biggest lever](/pages/breaking-the-spec.html) in precision equipment. It tilts the odds hard in your favour. It is not a pass or fail gate.

Plenty of instruments are sold by suppliers who were never named anywhere. Requirements are often written as performance criteria rather than a brand, and a competitor who can prove equivalence on accuracy, traceability and service can win on availability, lead time, local calibration support and a sharper commercial case. Budgets move. Specified suppliers lose to value engineering. The approved supplier list gets you considered, and a strong commercial case closes plenty of business from it.

So run both. Work the specification hard where you can influence it early, and keep a sharp approach for the enquiries you had no part in shaping. Just do not treat the tender as the start of the sale when there may have been a year of requirement writing before it.

## How to Build This Into a New Market

Three things, done deliberately.

- Map who writes the requirement in each target account, not just who signs the order. Lab manager, QA lead, test engineer, design authority.
- Put technical people in front of them early, with something useful to offer. A method review, a sample run, help with acceptance criteria.
- Make sure your channel partner in that market has the application and calibration depth to hold the conversation once you have opened it.

That last point is where a lot of manufacturers stall abroad. The partner can quote but cannot talk method with a lab manager, so the specification conversation never happens and the number plateaus. That is a capacity problem, not a product problem, and it can be fixed.

If you make precision kit and a market is not where you think it should be, start with **Qualification**. It is a paid yes or no call, direct with me, with a $250 refundable deposit. It is credited in full against Commercial Launchpad or the Fractional retainer if you go ahead, and refunded if I decide it is not the right fit. Or grab a 20 minute call and we will look at where the requirement is really being written in your target market.

items.title: Selling Instrumentation and Test Equipment: The Considered Buy
items.excerpt: In instrumentation and test there are always two buyers and they are never the same person. The engineer wants the capability, somebody else signs the capital, and most manufacturers arm the first then abandon them in front of the second. Here is how the considered buy actually works, and why calibration and service decide more export deals than accuracy ever does.
items.body:
Nobody signs off a test system because they liked the brochure.

Precision kit is a considered buy, and a considered buy has a shape. Miss the shape and you spend eighteen months being technically magnificent in front of somebody who cannot sign anything. I have sold precision [test and measurement](/pages/electronics-instrumentation-test.html) equipment into ST Microelectronics at around £100K and into Rescoll, and the Saab naval programme at $650K in Sweden and Nammo Raufoss at $500K in Norway came out of that same business. Different countries, different applications, same shape every time.

## The Engineer Wants It. Someone Else Signs It.

There are almost always two buyers and they are never the same person. There is the engineer, the lab manager or the QA lead who has the problem and wants the capability. Then there is whoever controls capital spend, who has never seen your instrument, does not care about your repeatability, and is weighing your machine against a new production line and a building repair.

Most manufacturers sell beautifully to the first person and abandon them completely in front of the second. The engineer becomes your unpaid internal salesperson and you hand them a data sheet to fight a capital case with. That is not a sale. That is a hope.

Arm them properly. Throughput gain in hours saved, the cost of the tests they currently send outside, the rework the capability prevents, a payback period written in the finance team's own language. An engineer left to build that case alone will do it badly, once, and then quietly stop trying.

> You are not selling an instrument. You are selling an engineer the argument they will have to win without you in the room.

## Your Real Competitor Is Usually Not Another Instrument

Manufacturers obsess about the rival brand. In a considered buy it is often the smallest threat in the room. Your real competition is the third party test house they already use, the old rig in the corner that still sort of works, and the decision to do nothing for another year. All three are cheaper than you this quarter. All three have an internal advocate. None appear on your competitor matrix.

So price against them. What does the customer spend a year sending samples out? What is that turnaround costing in delayed launches? What happens when the old rig fails a calibration and twelve months of test data comes into question? That is the comparison that moves capital, and almost nobody makes it for the customer.

## The Standard Sells the Instrument

This is the part precision manufacturers under use, and it is the most efficient thing you can do. A laboratory accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 does not get to choose whether it maintains metrological traceability. Clause 6.5 requires measurement results to be traceable to the SI system, with documented calibration, stated uncertainty and reference equipment kept current, and traceability is one of the most heavily scrutinised areas in an assessment. That is not your marketing claim. That is their obligation.

Same story in transit and packaging. A product package system tested to ASTM D4169 runs a defined distribution cycle and assurance level, with drop, vibration, compression and incline impact all specified, and the ISTA 2 and 3 series sit alongside it. Written down, publicly, by somebody who is not you.

When your kit exists to satisfy a written obligation, stop teaching your specification and start teaching the standard. Show the engineer how the requirement is met, what evidence an assessor will ask for, and where their current method leaves a gap. The standard creates the requirement. Your job is to be the obvious way to meet it.

## The Correlation Run Is the Real Tender

Every serious instrumentation sale ends in the same place. They put their own sample on your machine and compare the result to whatever they do now. Treat that as the tender, because it is.

Agree in advance what good looks like, what sample set is representative, who witnesses it, and what happens if the numbers differ from their existing method, because they will differ and the reason is usually that the old method was wrong. Without agreed acceptance criteria before the sample arrives you are not running a trial. You are giving a stranger a chance to fail your product on their terms.

Being written into the customer's internal test procedure or the project test method is the [biggest lever](/pages/breaking-the-spec.html) you have, and it tilts the odds hard. It is not a pass or fail gate though, and anyone telling you otherwise has not sold much. Plenty of instruments are bought from suppliers nobody named anywhere, on availability, lead time, local service reach and a sharper commercial case. The lever is worth fighting for. It is not the only door.

## Calibration and Service Decide the Export Deal

This is where good manufacturers lose export markets they should own. The purchase price is one line in a decision that also includes annual calibration, service response, spares, software licences, training and the downtime while the instrument is away being calibrated. At home all of that is invisible because it works. Four thousand miles away it is the whole argument.

Buyers in a new market ask four questions before they ask about accuracy:

- Who calibrates it here, and are they accredited for it
- How long is the instrument out of service when they do
- Who trains my people, and in what language
- What happens when it breaks in year three

If your answer to any of those is a flight from head office, you have handed the deal to a competitor with a local technical partner. The channel decision in precision equipment is technical, not commercial, which is why partners need scoring on calibration capability and engineering depth before you appoint them rather than after. [Parteloa](/pages/parteloa.html) handles that qualification work too. A distributor who can sell but cannot calibrate will cost you two years.

If you make instrumentation, test or precision electronics and a market has gone flat, the problem is rarely the instrument. It is usually that the capital case never got written, the standard never got taught, or the service answer never got built.

If you want a straight read on which of those is costing you, take the [Qualification](/pages/qualification.html). A paid yes or no call, direct with me, on a $250 refundable deposit.
